claims.text: Phase-selective recrystallization can improve the tensile ductility of eutectic alloys.
Phase-selective recrystallization alleviates dislocation pile-ups near lamellar phase boundaries.
Phase-selective recrystallization selectively recrystallizes the ductile phase.
Reducing interfacial dislocation pile-ups reduces stress concentrations and delays microcrack initiation.
Phase-selective recrystallization will retain or enhance strength relative to the untreated alloy.
The starting alloy consists of a soft FCC phase coupled with a harder B2/BCC phase in dual-phase lamellar colonies.
Semi-coherent internal boundaries in the starting alloy naturally develop dislocation pile-ups during deformation.
A controlled low-temperature, short-duration anneal can recrystallize the FCC phase without coarsening or dissolving the lamellar architecture.
The phase-selective recrystallization treatment forms equiaxed grains in the ductile phase.
Equiaxed grains in the ductile phase reduce sites for dislocation pile-up.
Retention of a skeletal hard-phase morphology maintains high strength.
Selective recrystallization relieves pre-existing dislocation substructures and minimizes dislocation accumulation at semi-coherent interfaces.
Reducing and confining early crack nucleation allows the strain-hardening capacity of the eutectic phases to be more fully used.
The maintained or refined hard-phase morphology continues to contribute to overall strength.
The treated alloy may achieve approximately twice the tensile elongation of the untreated alloy.
The treated alloy will match or slightly exceed the strength of the untreated alloy.
Limited room-temperature ductility and brittle behavior in the untreated alloy are largely caused by dislocation pile-ups at lamellar boundaries that initiate microcracking.
Excessive annealing can cause coarsening or loss of phase integrity and negate the benefits of phase-selective recrystallization.
